study.title: Isaiah 47 The fall of Babylon and the failure of its security
study.overview: Isaiah 47 announces the complete humiliation of Babylon, presented as a rather majestic city, now demolished to dust and bondage. The chapter shows that its ruin comes as a response to pride, cruelty against God's people, self-confidence and hidden practices in which it trusted. At the same time, the text states that the Lord, called the Redeemer and the Holy One of Israel, governs history and executes justice against oppression. The final message is that no ally, human counsel, or false spiritual power will be able to save it.

outline.title: Babylon is demoted from the throne to the dust
outline.explanation: The first verses describe the city as a virgin daughter now sitting on the ground, without throne, without delicacy and without honor. The image of the fall is public and shameful: it passes from the position of sovereign to that of a servant, exposed and without defense. At the center of the scene appears the confession that the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, is the Redeemer who does justice.

outline.title: The pride, cruelty and false security receive judgment
outline.explanation: Here the prophet explains why Babylon falls: she was an instrument of discipline against Israel, but treated the people with hardness and arrogance. The city boasted of eternal dominion, absolute security and exclusivity, as if no one could confront it. The text then announces that, in one coup, there will be loss of children and widowhood, in addition to unexpected and inevitable disaster, revealing that their wisdom and knowledge were deceptive.

outline.title: Enchanting and counselors cannot save
outline.explanation: Babylon is ironically invited to continue with its ancient practices, as if it could gain some benefit from them. Astrologers, observers from heaven and parents are called to help her, but all fail. The chapter ends by showing that such collaborators spread without direction and that no one remains to rescue it.

study.context: The chapter speaks of Babylon as the oppressive power judged by God. The notes highlight that the ruin announced is not mere human reviving, but part of divine justice: God punished Judah through Babylon and now judges Babylon itself for its violence, pride and trust in hidden practices. Matthew Henry also notes that the fall of Babylon serves to encourage the faith of God's people and can function as a figure of the collapse of a great enemy of God's people in the history of redemption.
study.theology: The chapter affirms God's sovereignty over empires, judgment, and history. The Lord not only sees oppression; he responds with righteousness, exposing the falsehood of human pride. The language of redemption in verse 4 is important: the same God who judges arrogance is also presented as the Redeemer and the Holy One of Israel. The text also denounces the idolatry of self-confidence: power, pleasure, human wisdom and hidden practices do not offer salvation. In Protestant evangelical perspective, this points to the inadequacy of any human security and the need to depend on the Lord who humiliates the proud and sustains his people.

scholarViews.insight: The expression "sit in the dust" total humiliation; Babylon, formerly exalted, is relegated to the place of a servant without honor.
The fall of Babylon is announced not to satisfy human vengeance, but to show that God's righteousness acts against its arrogance and to animate the faith of God's people.
The image of the delicate woman turned into a slave summarizes the denunciation of Babylon's destruction, culminating in the contrast between her past prosperity and her condition slaughtered.

questions: In what ways does the security of Babylon itself look like present forms of self-confidence without God?
Why does the text show that false power, knowledge, and spiritual practices cannot prevent judgment?
How is the confession that the Lord is the Redeemer in the midst of the proclamation of judgment strengthens the faith of God's people?
study.practice: This chapter calls on the believer to abandon all trust in prestige, resources, human predictions and self-power. The concrete application is to examine where our security is anchored: reputation, money, control, entertainment or human advice. He also calls us to reject any attempt to seek spiritual direction outside the Word of God. Instead of being proud, the disciple must live with reverence, humility and trust in the Lord who judges his people with justice and redeems his people.
study.uncertainty: The text and notes do not conclusively detail all the internal historical elements of Babylon's judgment, nor do they allow to identify with absolute certainty each image as an exclusive reference to a specific event. Notes also do not allow accurate fix dates, geography or further development than what was explicitly mentioned. Typological or confessional readings about a parallel with later church enemies should be understood as interpretation, not as a direct and indisputable statement of the verse.
